problem.text: How many ways are there to split the integers $1$ through $14$ into $7$ pairs so that in each pair the greater number is at least $2$ times the lesser number?

steps.title: Where to start: the big numbers cannot pair with each other
steps.body: Look at the numbers $8$ through $14$. If two of them formed a pair, the greater would have to be at least $2 \cdot 8 = 16$, which is too big. So each of these seven numbers needs its own partner from $1$ through $7$. There are exactly seven small numbers, so every pair is one small number with one large number.

your_turn.prompt: Why can $1$ and $2$ not be paired together, even though $2 \ge 2 \cdot 1$?
your_turn.answer: That would leave only $5$ small numbers for the $7$ large ones, so two large numbers would have to pair together, which is impossible.

steps.title: Start with the most restricted small number
steps.body: A small number $s$ needs a large partner that is at least $2s$. The number $7$ needs a partner of at least $14$, so it must pair with $14$. Handling the pickiest number first keeps the count simple, because each later number then has a fixed number of choices.

your_turn.prompt: After $7$ is paired with $14$, how many choices does $6$ have?
your_turn.answer: $2$: it needs at least $12$, so $12$ or $13$ ($14$ is taken).

steps.title: Keep going down the list
steps.body: The number $5$ needs at least $10$. That allows $10$ through $14$, minus the two already used, so $3$ choices. The number $4$ needs at least $8$, which allows all seven large numbers minus the three used, so $4$ choices. Careful: always subtract the partners already taken.

your_turn.prompt: Once $7$, $6$, $5$ and $4$ are paired, in how many ways can $1$, $2$ and $3$ take the three large numbers that are left?
your_turn.answer: $3! = 6$ ways. Every leftover number is at least $8$, which is at least $2 \cdot 3$, so any matching works.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.body:
Multiply the numbers of choices at each stage.
$$1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 4 \cdot 6 = 144$$
The answer is **(E)**.
